species.name: Capybara
species.description: The Capybara is the world’s largest rodent, commonly found in South American rainforests and wetlands. It is a semi-aquatic species that lives near rivers and lakes.
species.diet: Herbivorous, feeding mainly on grasses and aquatic plants.
species.habitat: Rainforest and wetlands near freshwater sources.
species.threats: Habitat loss, hunting for meat and hide, and water pollution.

species.name: Parrots
species.population: ≈ 393 species in 92 genera globally on iNaturalist
species.description: The order Psittaciformes includes all parrots, macaws, cockatoos and allied birds found mainly in tropical regions. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}
species.diet: Mostly seeds, nuts, fruits and some vegetation; many also use strong beaks for access and nest cavities.
species.habitat: Tropical and subtropical forests, woodlands, savannas and wetlands – many in rainforest biomes.
species.threats: Habitat loss, illegal pet trade, fragmentation, climate change.

species.name: Toco Toucan
species.description: The Toco Toucan is the largest and most recognizable toucan species, known for its massive orange bill and striking black and white plumage. It plays an important role in rainforest ecosystems as a seed disperser.
species.diet: Primarily fruits, but also insects, small reptiles, and eggs.
species.habitat: Tropical and subtropical rainforests, woodlands, and savannas of South America.
species.threats: Deforestation, habitat fragmentation, and illegal pet trade.

species.name: Jaguar
species.population: ≈ 5,000–15,000 mature individuals remaining in the wild
species.description: The Jaguar is the largest cat species in the Americas and an apex predator of the rainforest. Known for its powerful build and spotted coat, it plays a crucial role in maintaining ecological balance by regulating prey populations.
species.diet: Carnivorous; feeds on mammals, reptiles, birds, and fish — capable of piercing skulls and shells with its strong bite.
species.habitat: Tropical rainforests, wetlands, and dense riverine forests across Central and South America.
species.threats: Habitat loss, deforestation, poaching, and human-wildlife conflict.

species.name: Red-eyed Tree Frog
species.population: Widespread across Central and South America
species.description: The Red-eyed Tree Frog is one of the most iconic amphibians of the rainforest, easily recognized by its bright red eyes, vibrant green body, and blue-and-yellow striped sides. It is nocturnal and spends most of its life in trees near ponds and rivers.
species.diet: Carnivorous, feeding mainly on insects such as crickets, moths, and flies.
species.habitat: Lowland tropical rainforests, usually near freshwater sources for breeding.
species.threats: Habitat loss, deforestation, and climate change.
